course.title: Abdominal trauma
course.html:
Definitions

Traumatic lesion- Exchange of energies between victim and environment that goes beyond resistance body
Polytrauma- At least 2 different anatomical regions
- At least 1 has life risk
- Example: traumatized abdomen and limbs with spleen rupture
Poly-contusion- Lesions in several topographic regions without vital risk
Poly-fractures- Several fractures without involving vital prognosis

Etiology

  • External compressions - extreme intraabdominal pressure resulting in hollow organ ruptures
  • Abrupt decelerations - tear solid or hollow organs, especially mesenteries along vascular pedicles
  • Crushing - solid organs against posterior rigid abdominal wall (spine, ribs), intra- and retroperitoneal hemorrhages
  • Car accidents 50%
  • Work-related accidents 18%
  • Aggression 14%
  • Household accident 7%
  • Sports accidents 6%
  • Other causes (falls from heights) 5%

!!! The wound by the firearm has a complex pathogenesis

Classification of abdominal trauma

1. Closed abdominal trauma (contusions)
= blunt trauma		- 60-79% from abdominal trauma
- Mainly road accidents
2. Open abdominal trauma (wounds)A. Penetrating when vulnerable agent has entered peritoneal cavity
- Simple
- With visceral lesions
- With complex lesions: neighboring anatomical areas (thoraco-
abdominal, abdominal-pelvis, thoracic-abdominal-pelvic wounds)
B. Non-penetrating, when they do not enter peritoneal cavity
Incidence of visceral lesions in abdominal woundsIncidence of visceral lesions in abdominal contusions
- Small intestine 26%
- Large intestine 14%
- Spleen 7%
- Pancreas 3-5%
- Diaphragm muscles 3-5%		- Small intestine 16%
- Liver 15%
- Diaphragm muscles 1-3%
- Pancreas 1-3%

Location can indicate affected organs

  • Midline sterno-abdominal contusions - aorta, heart, spleen, left hepatic lobe and small bowel
  • Left lateral impacts - left lung, spleen, left kidney
  • Right lateral impacts - right lung, right hepatic lobe, right kidney

Wound’s classification

Depending on traumatic agenta) By cutting
b) By shooting
c) Contusion
Depending on age, wounds may bea) Recent (less than 6 hours)
b) Old (more than 6 hours)
Depending on microbial contamination,
they can be		a) Clean
b) With minimal contamination
c) Contaminated
d) Infected

Topographic classification

  • Solitary abdominal trauma
  • Lower abdominal trauma, usually associated with pelvic fracture
  • Abdominal parietal
  • Abdominal parieto-visceral
  • Abdominal wall trauma
  • Thoraco-abdominal trauma (trauma affecting the space between the 5th rib → costal rim)
  • Extra-abdominal lesion associations

Clinical manifestation

Peritoneal irritation syndrome- Distended abdomen
- Muscular defense or not (tenderness, guarding)
- Abdomen motionless with breath
- Sensitive Douglas pouch
- Disappearance of liver dullness
Internal bleeding syndrome- Agitation
- Anxiety
- Thirst
- Pallor
- Tachycardia
- Decreasing BP
- Shock
Mixed syndrome

Physical exam

Local exam- Overall appearance, immobility with breathing, retraction or distension
- Skin changes: abrasion, bruises – “traumatic mark”
Percussion- It is painful; Mandel sign → peritoneal irritations
- Disappearance of liver dullness → cavity organ immunity
- Dullness is movable on flanks (shifting dullness) → peritoneal effusion
Palpation- Temperature, elasticity and humidity of skin
- Cold skin, corroborated with pallor found at shock
- Fixed, firm, painful kneading → intraperitoneal hematoma
- Subcutaneous fluctuating collections
Signs
- Muscular defense (tenderness)
- Muscle contractions → permanent generalized beyond self-control (guarding)
! false acute abdominal trauma!
- Muscle ruptures
- Retroperitoneal hematoma
- Irritation of roots on nerves D2-D12
- Basal pneumonia
- Blumberg sign
Auscultation- Absence of intestinal noise → 65-93% sign of visceral lesions

Paraclinical exam

  • Laboratory exam
  • Chest and abdominal radiography (spleen rupture or liver rupture)
  • Abdominal US (FAST)
  • CT (best method)
  • Selective arteriography
  • Urography
  • Peritoneal lavage with 200-300 ml saline (in pat. with negative FAST US) to see bile, food of blood

General treatment approach

  • Primary evaluation
  • RAPID – SYSTEMATIC - THOROUGH in order to detect immediately life-threatening lesions !
  • Primary survey (ABC), anamnesis, brief physical examination, signs of hypovolemia/ hemorrhage/ hemodynamic instability
  • Situations that hide acute abdominal lesion: altered mental status (brain lesions, shock, intoxication), chest bowl injury, severe external lesions (open limb fractures)
  • Signs of instability: tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, acidosis
  • FAST US for presents of free fluid (hemoperitoneum, pericardial, pleural fluid, pneumothorax)
  • In negativ US → thorough search for other possible bleeding sources !
  • Patient’s stabilization
  • Venous access, massive transfusions, transfusion ratio 1:1:1 Plasma: red cells: platelets
  • Secondary evaluation
  • Other imaging
  • KEHR – abdominal pain irradiated to left shoulder, left thoraco-abdominal trauma → signifies splenic rupture
  • CULLEN – periumbilical ecchymosis – retro/properitoneal hematoma
  • TURNER – uni-or bilateral flanks ecchymosis – retroperitoneal hematoma
  • SEATBELT SIGN – skin abrasions, erytema, erosions; pancreatic, duodenal, small bowel, mesentery lesions, T12-L2 fracture; neck or cervical vessel lesions
  • Solid organs - hemoperitoneum; spleen and liver generate intra-peritoneal bleedings
  • Kidneys and pancreas - retroperitoneal hematomas
  • Hollow viscera - localized or diffuse peritonitis
  • Vascular - hemorrhagic shock due to intaperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding
  • Definitive care
  • Initial truncated surgical procedure focused exclusively on immediate life-threatening lesions → no longer than 1 hour
  • After 24-48 hours of postoperative resuscitation → programmed final reoperation follows with removal of initially placed intra-abdominal hemostatic packs, reparations of visceral damages, abdominal wall reconstruction
  • Liver ruptures will be packed, lacerated spleen will be resected, important vascular structures will be ligated
  • Massive Transfusion Protocol
  • Simple sutures of ruptured bowels or urinary bladder, rapid resection of largely compromised bowel loops followed by temporary stappled-closing of bowels’ ends, never reconstructive anastomosis!
  • Brief peritoneal lavage with warm normal saline, bowels exteriorized and all 4 abdominal quadrants temporarily packed → prevents intraabdominal postoperative diffuse bleedings due to coagulopathy
  • Suturing abdominal wall not indicated; temporary closure by vacuum device
  • Often develop very severe combination of metabolic deregulations = “lethal triad” (hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy)
  • Monitored, ventilated, corrected, aggressive large-spectrum antibiotherapy and total par-enteral nutrition
1. Closed abdominal traumatism
1. Patient
hemodynamically
unstable and peritoneal
signs which goes directly
into operating room		- Intubated or unconscious patient
- Patients with “belt mark”
- US
- Peritoneal lavage. (1000 erythrocytes is criteria for performing
exploratory laparoscopy. This can reduce rate of negative laparotomies by
up to 10%)
- In absence of ultrasound in receiving area it is sent directly to operating
room
2. Stable hemodynamic
pat.		- Abdominal US
- CT

Indications for surgery

  • Hypotension
  • Peritonitis
  • Hypotension despite rebalancing
  • Pneumoperitoneum
  • Diaphragm injury
  • Intraperitoneal rupture of urinary bladder
  • CT or US diagnosis of severe traumatic lesions of pancreas, spleen, liver, kidney or gastrointestinal tract

Open abdominal traumatism

Hepatic trauma

  • Large organ, parenchymal → easily injured
  • Liver is only partially protected by the right hypochondrium

Clinical signs

  • Pain in right hypochondrium
  • Peritoneal irritation
  • Hypotension – collapse
  • Psychic signs
  • Signs of hemobility
Grade I- Subcapsular hematoma < 10% of surface
- Plague < 1cm deep
Grade II- Subcapsular hematoma 10-50% of surface or intra parenchyma <10cm diameter
- Wound 1-3cm deep and < 10cm long
Grade III- Subcapsular, > 50% of liver surface or growing; subcapsular or intra parenchyma ruptured hematoma;
intraparenchymal hematoma > 10cm
- Wound > 3cm deep
Grade IV- Wound: rupture of parenchyma involving 25-75% of hepatic lobe or 1-3 Couinaud segments in single
lobe
Grade V- Wound: rupture of parenchyma involving> 75% of lobe or > 3 Couinaud segments of single lobe
- Vascular: suprahepatic lesions, vein retrohepatic vein. Major hepatic hepatitis
Grade I→ Small laceration with minimal bleeding
Treatment: Usually bleeding has ceased at laparotomy; drainage is sufficient
Grade II→ Moderate laceration with active and significant bleeding
Treatment: Compression, argon beam coagulation, bipolar coagulation, radiofrequency, fibrin glue
Grade III→ Large intraparenchymal hematomas
Treatment: Intraoperative drainage and hemostasis is mandatory
Grade IV→ Large lacerations with transection of identifiable intrahepatic branches of hepatic artery, portal vein,
hepatic vein or bile ducts, but amenable to suture repair
Treatment: Pringle maneuver necessary during surgery and visible affected elements must be
separately ligated. Ligation of proper or common hepatic artery has been largely abandoned as is may
lead to abscess formation
Grade V→ Large lacerations with transection of identifiable intrahepatic branches of hepatic artery, portal vein,
hepatic vein or bile ducts
Treatment: Requiring resection of portion of hepatic parenchyma
Grade VILarge lacerations associated with injury of retrohepatic veins and vena cava resulting in massive
hemorrhage
Treatment: Sometimes total vascular exclusion may be necessary to visualize and suture injuries to
hepatic veins and VCI. To gain access to suprahepatic VCI it is necessary to extend midline incision into
mediastinum by splitting sternum

Treatment

Conservative- Only hemodynamically stable ones (gr. I-III)
- CT monitoring
Surgical- Hepatorafia
- Plumbing fill
- Typical or atypical hepatectomies
- Vascular sutures
- Sutures of biliary tract
  • Additional surgical procedures may be required due to intra- and extra-abdominal injuries
  • Stab wounds cause mainly minor injuries (Types I-III)
  • Gunshots and blunt trauma cause serious injuries (Types IV-VI) in half of these situations
  • Preoperative assessment includes ultrasound, CT scan, puncture lavage
  • Complications of liver trauma include abscesses, biliary fistulae, hemobilia, liver failure, secondary bleeding,

parenchymal necrosis

  • Hemobilia is defined a bleeding draining in the biliary tree with subsequent biliary colic, raised cholestasis enzymes

and melena

  • Arteriography may be of help by detecting the source and obtaining hemostasis by selective embolization

Splenic trauma

  • Most affected viscera in abdominal trauma

Signs and symptoms

  • Left hypochondrial pain
  • Signs of acute anemia
  • Kehr sign (irradiated pain in the left shoulder)
  • Abdominal distension
  • Contracting
  • Left or displaceable hypochondriac

Severity of splenic trauma

I- Non-expanding subcapsular hematoma <10% of the surface
- Wound without bleeding <1 cm depth
II- Non-expanding subcapsular hematoma, <10-50% of the surface
- Non-expanding intra-parenchymatous hematoma with diameter <2 cm
- Capsular lesion with active bleeding
- Parenchymal lesion with a depth of 1-3 cm that does not involve the trabecular vessels
III- Subcapsular hematoma> 50% of the surface or expansively
- Subcapsular hematoma ruptured, with active bleeding
- Hematoma intra-parenchymatos with diameter> 2 cm or expansive
- Parenchymal lesion> 3 cm or with trabecular vessel damage
IV- Broken intraparenchymal hematoma, with active bleeding
- Injury involving the segmental or spleen vessels, with the production of major
devascularization (> 25% of the spleen)
V- Crushing of the spleen
- Avulsion

Treatment

Non-surgical- Conservative
- Embolization of vessels
Surgical= classic/ laparoscopic
- Partial splenectomy
- Splenectomy

Stomach

  • Most common affected in abdominal wounds of left hypochondrium
  • In contusions by crushing steering wheel
  • Clinical signs of peritoneal irritation
  • Pneumoperitoneum (cavity organ)

Injury grade

ISingle wall injury
IIPenetrating lesion
IIIMinor parietal destruction
IVInjury requiring minimal resection
VInjury requiring resection of more than 35% of the stomach

Treatment (depending on lesion)

  • 1. Wound suture
  • 2. Gastric resection
  • 3. Gastrectomy

Pancreas

  • More common in wounds
  • Difficult to diagnose → late clinical signs
  • Delayed diagnosis → late interventions lead to increased morbidity and mortality

Treatment

I- Conservative treatment
- Drainage
II
IIIIII- Distal pancreatectomy
- Drainage
IV- Subtotal pancreatectomy
- Drainage
V- Cephalic Duodeno-pancreatectomy
- Cephalic pancreatectomy

Duodenum

  • Rare lesions
  • Usually coexists with other visceral lesions (90% of cases)
  • Pain
  • Muscular defense

Injury grade

I- Hematoma of a single portion of the duodenum
- Incomplete wound
II- Hematoma involving more than one portion
- Wound: 50% of the circumference
III- Wound: 50-75% the circumference of D II
- Or 50-100% of the circumference D I, D III, D IV
IV- Break> 75% of circumference D II, involving the ampule or distal common duct
VV- Massive rupture of the duodeno-pancreatic complex
- Devascularization of the duodenum

Treatment

  • Decompressive duodenal drainage
  • Anastomosis and resection
  • Pedicle graft
  • Duodenal resections
  • Cephalic duodeno-pancreatectomy

Colon and rectum

  • More affected in abdominal wounds

Signs

  • Perforation of the visceral cavity
  • Pneumoperitoneum
  • Hemoperitoneum

Injury grade

ISerosa injury
IISingle parietal lesion
IIILess than 25% of the wall
IVMore than 25% of the wall
VMajor involvement of colonic wall and blood supply

Treatment

  • Wound suture
  • Segmental resections
  • Hemicolectomy
  • Colostomy
  • Suture of rectal lesion + colostomy

Aorta and vena cava

  • They are rare, usually by stabbing or firearms
  • Signs of severe acute anemia
  • Needs urgent intervention
  • Vascular wound repair

Gun wound

Unipolar/ blind wound- Only in form of penetration hole
- Projectile remained in tissues
Bipolar wound- Projectile inlet and outlet port
- If you are only interested in superficial plans, it is called wound in seton

Areas of trauma

  • Channel itself
  • Primary necrosis area
  • Molecular contusion

book.html:
Abdominal trauma

Doru Munteanu

ETIO-PATHOGENY

There arethree main machanisms involvedin abdominaltraumatisms (AT): ●external compressions – generate extreme values of intraabdominal pressure, resulting usually in hollow organs’ ruptures; ●abrupt decelerations, tear solid organs or hollow organs, and especially mesenteries along with vascular pedicles; ●crushings, especially solid organs against the posterior rigid abdominal wall (spine, ribs), generate intra- and retroperitoneal hemorrhages.

From the point of view of the traumatic agent, AT can be divided in – Blunt traumatisms

  • Abdominal wounds

Both the above-mentioned categories can be further subdivided according to the underlying visceral involvement. Blunt traumatisms can generate exclusively abdominal parietal damages, without any visceral involvement (parietal blunt abdominal trauma, resulting in abdominal wall hematomas), or present associated uni- or multi-visceral damages. Open abdominal traumatisms may as well involve exclusively abdominal parietal structures (with two subdivisions, namely non-penetrating wounds, e.g., the ones that respect the peritoneal layer, and penetrating wounds, the ones with involvement of the parietal peritoneum; these last ones, do not necessary generate visceral injuries – the so-called abdominal parietal penetrating wounds -which, when large enough,may result in eviscerations. Abdominal penetrating wounds with visceraldamages, are named abdominal parietovisceral wounds.

Causes: the most frequent causes for AT are: - Motor vehicles collisions (75%) (MVC)

  • Falls from hight
  • Aggressions
  • Sports.

In unrestrained MVCs knowing the part of torso involved, may help the medical team from the ED to anticipate a certain pattern of lesions, as follows: in midline sterno-abdominal contusions, the aorta, heart, spleen, left hepatic lobe and small bowel are more likely to be involved; left lateral impacts, left lung, spleen, left kidney are more frequently affected, while in right lateral impacts, the right lung, the right hepatic lobe, and right kidney are injured.

  • In a general classification by the frequence of injuries, the spleen is the

most frequently injured abdominal organ, followed by the liver, the kidneys, small bowel, mesentery, colon and rectum, diaphragm, pancreas and major vessels.

Management of AT

Four steps have to be respected, according to the Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol:

I. Primary evaluation

II. Patient’s stabilization

III. Secondary evaluation

VI. Definitive care.

I. Initial evaluation of an acutely injured patient has to be:

RAPID

SYSTEMATIC

THOROUGH in order to detect immediately life-threatening lesions!

During this primary survey, anamnesis, a local and general brief physical examination is carried out, searching for signs of peritoneal irritation (pain abdominal tenderness/guarding), clinical signs of intra-abdominal hemorrhage, hypovolemia, hemodynamic instability (pallor, blood pressure, pulse rate). If there are no clinical signs of acute abdomen and the patient is stabile, with normal blood tests and imaging, the patient can be discharged with indications for prompt readmission in case if any of the complaints recurrs. Care must be taken, as there are some particular circumstances that may mask/hide abdominal internal lesions: - Altered mental status (concomitant brain lesions, severe shock, intoxications (alcohol, drugs);

  • Concomitant chest wall injuries (do not exhibit abdominal pain or

tenderness).

  • Impressive external lesions (e,g, open limb fractures – may derive

attention from an abdominal silent bleeding!).

  • - Patient becoming unstable: (presents tachycardia, hypotension,

oliguria, acidosis), reflects an ongoing hemorrhage: - Abdominal Trauma Life Support protocols for initial resuscitation :

  • Airways and normal Breathing must be maintained, along with

hemodynamic stability – Circulation -(A,B,C) – High flow oxygen, early intubation (especially in patients with severe politrauma or at high risk for imminent instability);

  • Large venous peripheric catheters/central venous catheter
  • These patients need prompt massive transfusions (i.e., 10 or more units

of packed red blood cells within 24 hour period); ideally, a balanced transfusion ratio of 1:1:1: of plasma to red blood cells to platelets (in these patients with severe coagulopathy!) will contribute to a decreased mortality.

-If proper clinical or radiological evaluation is not possible in extremis, even early placement of a chest tube (in diagnostic purpose, and, when suspicion of concomitant thoracic bleeding, therapeutic) can be helpful.

Yet, clinical examination misses up to 45% of abdominal lesions, thus a bedside abdominal ultrasonography is performed, according to the F.A.S.T. protocol (Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma). The initial indications where to evaluate the presence of abdominal free fluid, especially in unstabile patients with blunt trauma suspected of having hemoperitoneum; there are several advantages:- it is an excellent triage tool for unstable patients;

  • bedside availability
  • it is noninvasive
  • it is a fast procedure (takes only 2 minutes!)
  • detects pericardial and pleural fluid collections.

The indications have now been extended (eFAST), for evaluation of lungs for pneumothorax.

Hemodynamically unstable patients with positive results(hemoperitoneum confirmed) will be sent immediately to the OR for laparatomy; in hemodynamically unstable patients with negative or equivocal results after FAST, Diagnostic Peritoneal Lavage may help.

D.P.L.: After naso-gastric tube and a urinary catheter insertion, a No.11 catheter is introduced through a needle into the abdomen, subombilically; the result is positive if●10ml of fresh blood are obtained at aspiration (hemoperitoneum confirmed although in small amount); if not, 1 L of warm normal saline is instilled through the catheter intra-peritoneally and subsequently drained out through declivity (diagnostic peritoneal lavage); positive result if ●100.000 RBC/mm³ are detected (or ● >500WBC/mm³ in case of peritonitis); ●if bile, or ●alimentary particles are exteriorized.

If a suspected hemoperitoneum in an unstable patient is not

confirmed by FAST, a thoroughsearch for other possible bleeding

sources is carried out!(thorax, pelvis,fractures).

II. Initial efficient and persistent stabilization allows for further investigations.

III. Stabile (or stabilized) patients: can be further completely, (physically and radiologically), examined and explored and subsequently mobilized (passively) and sent for CT scan, X-rays, etc.

CT is the most accurate imaging technique as it not only establishes with high sensibility and specificity the diagnosis of acute abdomen (hemorrhagic or peritonitic type), but it is superior to ultrasound in detecting the underlying injured viscera.

Clinical signs in blunt abdominal injuries:- KEHR – abdominal pain irradiated to the left shoulder, in a patient with left lateral thoraco-abdominal trauma – signifies an underlying splenic rupture;

  • CULLEN – periumbilical ecchymosis – retro/properitoneal hematoma;
  • TURNER – uni-or bilateral flanks ecchymosis –retroperitoneal

hematoma. (These signs however usually are late ones as these ecchymosesmay appear days after the initial trauma with retroperitoneal subsequent hematoma).

  • SEATBELT SIGN – there are skin abrasions, erytema, and erosions in

a pattern of a seatbelt; the importance of this sign resides in the fact that it is associated, (in the “lap belt” variant which is very rare nowadays - in over 50% of the cases with severe abdominal - pancreatic, duodenal, small bowel, mesentery lesions - , as well as with a typical spine - T12-L2 - fracture (Chance fracture); cervical seatbelt sign is associated with neck or cervical vessels’ lesions.

  • Regarding the clinical manifestations of AT the following affected

structures can be systemathised: - The abdominal wall

  • Solid organs (spleen, pancreas, liver, kidneys)
  • Hollow organs (Stomach, small/large bowel, urinary bladder)
  • Vascular structures.

Each of the above-mentioned structures can be isolated or combined, associated, injured, generating more or less recognizable clinical patterns: Solid organs, are more or less made of sponge-like tissues, very well vascularised, thus their lacerations will always generate intra-abdominal hemorrhages (hemoperitoneum); spleen and liver will generate intraperitoneal bleedings, with severity scores ranging (depending on the complexity and extension of the lesion) from a simple, minimal hemoperitoneum, with no hemodynamic and biologic consequences, with spontaneous healing, to fulminant, highly lethal ones (grade 5 lesions). Kidneys and pancreas will often generate retroperitoneal hematomas, sometimes very voluminous, with consecutive impressive and persistant bowel’s paresis and abdominal distension.

  • Hollow viscera, due to their irritating and septic, contaminating

content, once ruptured or perforated, will generate localized or diffuseperitonitis, with the typical clinical features.

–Vascular structures, depending on their nature (arteries or veins), their caliber (small, medium or large vessels), and their location (inta-peritoneally or retro-peritoneally), will generate hemorrhagic shock, due to intaperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding. Well, in real life, these lesions are not so well systematized; usually there is a more or less complex combination and the result will be an aggravating association, basically between haemorrhage and peritonitis.

IV.Definitive care - is the natural next step; patients are now sent to the ICU or to the OR, according to the clinical and radiological findings.

Patients presenting with signs of severe ongoing bleeding, hemodynamically unstable at presentation, or who become unstable after initial stabilization, pacients requiring massive blood transfusions, are candidates for immediate surgical exploration. The particularities of these very vulnerable cases have imposed, since the early 90’s, a special concept, named “damage control surgery” (Rotondo, 1993). It consists of an initial truncated surgical procedure, focused exclusively on the immediate lifethreatening lesions (the hemorrhagic and the contaminating ones). After 2448 hours of vigorous postoperative resuscitation in the intensive care unit, a programmed final reoperation follows, with removal of initially placed intra-abdominal hemostatic packs, reparations of the previously deliberately abandoned visceral damages (anastomoses, stomies), and definitive abdominal wall reconstruction.

  • Thus the initial surgical exploration should not last more than 1 hour.

The main goal is to promptly control all hemorrhagic sources; liver ruptures will be packed, largely lacerated spleen will be resected, important vascular structures will be ligated (or sutured), etc. At the same time, the Massive Transfusion Protocol goes on; once the haemostatic maneuvers have been accomplished, the blood pressure starts promptly to return to normal values and the patient becomes hemodynamically stabilized. Dealing with the septic contaminating sources comes next, yet only simple, time-saving maneuvers are allowed for the moment (simple sutures of ruptured bowels or urinary bladder, rapid resection of largely compromised bowel loops -followed by temporary stappled-closing of the bowels’ ends, and by no means a reconstructive anastomosis!). After a brief peritoneal lavage with warm normal saline, the bowels will be exteriorized and all four abdominal quadrants will be temporarily packed; this maneuver is important in order to prevent intra abdominal postoperative diffuse bleedings due to a persistent coagulopathy. Suturing the abdominal wall is not indicated for the time being; temporary abdominal closure using a vacuum device is preferred in this setting.

  • Postoperative resuscitation is of crucial importance now, as despite the

initial stabilization, these patients will, if not already, develop a very severe combination of metabolic deregulations, generally known as the “lethal triad” (hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy). Hence, the next 24-48 hours, these patients will be thoroughly sustained, monitored, ventilated, all altered biological parameters will be thoroughly corrected, concomitant with an aggressive large-spectrum antibiotherapy and total par-enteral nutrition.

  • Take-back final operation is carried out, but only after the efficient

correction of all major metabolic and physiologic deep deregulations has been accomplished. After removal of the abdominal wall vacuum device, a new thorough exploration of the abdominal cavity is carried out; all the previously hemostatic swabs or packs must be counted and removed; all the previously unresolved lesions will now be repaired (e.g., continuity of the digestive tract is reestablished); after another final peritoneal washing with warm normal saline, the definitive closing of the abdominal fascia is performed.
